definition: Respite means a short period of rest or relief from something difficult.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word respite. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know respite should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The ceasefire gave the border villages a two-week respite, long enough to bring in the harvest.
A breather is seconds or minutes snatched mid-effort; respite goes further — a real stretch of relief in which the pressure genuinely lifts.
Deliverance goes far beyond respite: a respite ends and the hardship returns, while deliverance means being rescued from it once and for all.

A reprieve is relief that someone with power grants — the execution stayed, the deadline pushed back, the closure postponed. It comes down from a decision. A respite needs no one's signature: the shelling pauses, the fever breaks, the pain lets up. Both are temporary; only a reprieve is issued.

A lull is a quiet spell in the activity itself — the wind drops, the shelling thins, the orders stop coming in. It is measured from outside and need not be felt as relief by anyone. A respite is defined by the sufferer: relief from hardship, felt as relief, with the hardship waiting.

Nobody mistook it for the end of the rains — the second front was already on the forecast.

Respite is more exact than break because it requires hardship on both sides of it: a coffee break interrupts an ordinary morning, but a respite is carved out of something genuinely punishing, and everyone knows the punishment resumes.
Respite needs hardship to push against: heat, grief, shelling, double shifts.
For a pause with nothing painful around it, break or lull is the honest word.
Its cluster-mate repose is the resting itself — during a respite from the grind, you might finally repose.

For two years Lena's alarm had gone off every three hours, around the clock, so she could check on her father.
When her aunt flew in for ten days and took over the night shifts, Lena did not know what to do with the silence at first.
She slept, then slept more.
She saw a film in a theater.
She read forty pages of a paperback without listening for footsteps.
The whole visit, she knew, was a respite and not a rescue: the flight home was already booked, and the alarm would return to her nightstand.
But relief that is temporary, her aunt insisted, is still relief — and Lena flew through her days like proof.
